item.title: The 61 days that changed Bangladesh
item.description:
What began as a student demand to reform government job quotas rapidly evolved into the largest political upheaval in Bangladesh’s modern history, ending 15 years of uninterrupted Awami League rule and forcing then prime minister Sheikh Hasina from office.
Two years later, the July Uprising remains one of the country’s defining political turning points, not only because it toppled a government that had appeared electorally unassailable, but because it transformed a limited campus movement into a nationwide revolt against authoritarian rule, police violence and shrinking democratic space.
The movement unfolded with remarkable speed.
In just 61 days, Bangladesh went from a seemingly stable post-election government to a political transition that redrew the country’s landscape.
The immediate trigger came on June 5, 2024, when the High Court reinstated quotas for descendants of freedom fighters in government recruitment, reversing a system abolished in 2018.
Students at Dhaka University launched protests the next day, soon joined by universities across the country.
Initially, protesters focused solely on quota reform.
By early July, however, the newly formed Students Against Discrimination platform had begun coordinating nationwide demonstrations, road blockades and the “Bangla Blockade” program after the Appellate Division declined to suspend the High Court verdict.
Despite growing protests, senior government leaders dismissed the movement, insisting the issue would be resolved through the courts.
The confrontation entered a decisive phase on July 14 when Sheikh Hasina publicly addressed the issue for the first time.
Responding to a question, she asked whether government jobs should go to “the grandchildren of collaborators” if they were not reserved for descendants of freedom fighters.
The remark, widely interpreted by protesters as branding them “Rajakars,” fundamentally changed the movement.
Within hours, students marched through campuses chanting, “We wanted our rights, and we became Rajakars.”
The slogan became one of the defining symbols of the uprising.
The following day, clashes erupted after Chhatra League leaders vowed to confront protesters.
Violence spread across Dhaka University, leaving hundreds injured and marking the point at which the quota movement transformed into a broader confrontation with the state.
On July 16, police gunfire killed Begum Rokeya University student Abu Sayed, the first widely recognised martyr of the movement.
Images of his final moments quickly spread nationwide, galvanising public support and drawing thousands more into the protests.
Over the following days, violence escalated dramatically.
Border Guard Bangladesh was deployed, a nationwide curfew imposed, the army called out and internet services shut down as security forces attempted to contain the unrest.
Although the Supreme Court ultimately overturned the High Court ruling on July 21 and restored a largely merit-based quota system, the movement no longer centred on quotas.
By then, protesters were demanding accountability for the killings, the release of detained coordinators, an end to mass arrests and, increasingly, the resignation of Sheikh Hasina herself.
Authorities detained several key coordinators of the Students Against Discrimination platform, including Nahid Islam, Asif Mahmud, Abu Baker Mojumder, Sarjis Alam, Hasnat Abdullah and Nusrat Tabassum.
Protest leaders alleged some were forced to announce the withdrawal of the movement while in custody, accusations that further fuelled public anger.
As Facebook profile pictures turned red in memory of those killed, the movement shifted from “March for Justice” to its final mobilization, “March to Dhaka.”
On August 5, tens of thousands of protesters converged on the capital despite curfew restrictions and security deployments.
By early afternoon, Sheikh Hasina had left the country for India.
Army chief General Waker-uz-Zaman announced that an interim government would assume responsibility for governing the country.
The fall of the government triggered celebrations across Bangladesh, while crowds entered Ganabhaban and attacks were reported on police stations, Awami League offices and other state-linked facilities.
Two years on, the human cost of the uprising remains disputed.
The July Uprising Directorate currently recognises 843 July martyrs, while the July Martyrs’ Memorial Foundation has published more than 820 verified fatalities.
Other organisations have claimed significantly higher death tolls.
What remains beyond dispute is the speed with which Bangladesh’s political trajectory changed.
In just two months, a movement born from a recruitment policy dispute evolved into a nationwide uprising that ended one of the country’s longest-serving governments and reshaped its political future.

item.title: Two years after July revolution, hope meets hard reality
item.description:
Two years after the July 2024 uprising reshaped Bangladesh’s political landscape, many of the students who helped lead the movement say the country has yet to deliver the deep institutional reforms they believed they were fighting for.
While many credit the uprising with ending an era of authoritarian politics and awakening a new generation politically, students who took part in the movement say the structural reforms they fought for have yet to materialize, with corruption, insecurity, intolerance and weak governance continuing to shape public life.
Their reflections also find support in recent data.
Transparency International Bangladesh’s latest National Household Survey reported that citizens’ experiences of corruption while accessing public services have increased since the political transition, raising fresh questions about whether changes in government have translated into meaningful reforms within state institutions.
For many students, the movement was never solely about removing a government.
They say it represented a demand for a more accountable state, independent institutions, equal opportunities, democratic freedoms and an end to discrimination.
Two years later, many believe those ambitions remain only partially fulfilled.
“There has been no meaningful transformation in the economy, education, society or culture,” said Sajib Ahmed Zenich, a student at Jahangirnagar University.
“The expectations that brought students onto the streets have largely remained unmet. Economic hardship has deepened, unemployment remains a major concern and many of the structural reforms we hoped for have yet to materialise.”
Even so, he does not regard the uprising as a failure.
“The July uprising is not the final chapter. It will continue to inspire future struggles against inequality.”
Other students argue that although people today enjoy greater freedom to express opinions than before, institutional reform has lagged behind political change.
Wali Al Masud, another Jahangirnagar University student, said corruption, religious intolerance and violence continue to cast doubt on whether the political transition has fundamentally altered governance.
“People may speak more freely than before, but many still face intimidation for expressing different opinions,” he said.
For Dhaka University student Tamzid Haider, the July uprising represented the culmination of nearly two decades of accumulated public frustration over the erosion of democratic rights.
He believes many of the grievances that fuelled the protests, including demands for accountability and justice, remain unresolved.
“The trials over the July killings have not progressed as people expected,” he said.
“There has also been an increase in mob violence and attacks on minorities and people holding different opinions. These developments raise difficult questions about how much has truly changed.”
Several female students said one of the most disappointing developments has been the rise in online harassment and intimidation targeting women.
Shabnam Akter said many women who actively participated in the uprising have since withdrawn from public engagement because of cyberbullying and organised online attacks.
Dhaka University student Sheikh Tasnim Afroze Emi echoed those concerns, saying the increase in online abuse and mob behaviour has created fresh insecurity for women despite their prominent role during the movement.
Others expressed disappointment that some student leaders who inspired the protests have become increasingly distant from ordinary people’s concerns after the political transition.
Yet despite widespread frustration, almost none of those interviewed questioned the historical significance of the uprising itself.
Instead, they described it as the beginning of a much longer struggle.
Many believe its greatest achievement was not the transfer of political power but the emergence of a generation more willing to question authority, demand accountability and participate in public affairs.
For them, the real test of July will not be whether it changed a government in 2024, but whether it ultimately succeeds in transforming the institutions and political culture that inspired thousands of young people to take to the streets in the first place.

item.title: Two years on, a July fighter waits to see again
item.description:
On August 5, 2024, 20-year-old madrasa student Abu Hanif stepped into a procession in Narayanganj believing he was joining thousands demanding justice, dignity and reform.
Moments later, a rubber bullet struck his right eye.
The retina was torn. The vision was gone forever.
Two years after the July Uprising reshaped Bangladesh’s political landscape, Hanif’s life remains frozen on that afternoon in Chashara, where he lost not only the sight in one eye but also the ordinary future he had imagined.
While the country marks the uprising’s second anniversary, hundreds of injured protesters continue to live with permanent disabilities, prolonged treatment and uncertain rehabilitation.
“I cannot see anything with my right eye,” Hanif told Dhaka Tribune.
“Whenever I go outside, my eyes start itching. I cannot study for long. Sometimes the pain spreads from my eye to my head. Every day is painful.”
Originally from Khairaki village in Ishwarganj, Mymensingh, Hanif was then studying at Jamia Usman Ibn Affan (RA) Al Islamia Qawmi Madrasa in Narayanganj.
He said he had initially stayed away from the movement.
But the killing of Begum Rokeya University student Abu Sayed and repeated attacks on protesters convinced him he could no longer remain silent.
On August 5, Hanif joined thousands of demonstrators in Narayanganj.
He said he watched a fellow protester being shot dead before a rubber bullet hit his own eye.
Friends rushed him first to a nearby pharmacy before taking him to safety.
After news spread that Sheikh Hasina had resigned, he was admitted to the National Institute of Ophthalmology.
Emergency surgery could not save his vision.
Doctors later informed him that the sight in his right eye could never be restored.
Two additional operations also failed to improve his condition.
Hanif now studies at Jamia Muhammadiya Shamsul Uloom Madrasa in Savar, but says persistent pain, excessive tearing and blurred vision in his remaining eye often prevent him from concentrating.
Regular medication has also become another struggle.
“Some medicines are available at the hospital, but many have to be bought from outside,” he said.
Despite everything, he has not abandoned hope.
Doctors abroad, he said, have indicated that advanced treatment might restore at least part of his vision.
“I have been told that if I can receive treatment abroad, there is still hope,” he said.
“But my family cannot afford it. During the interim government I tried many times to get permission for treatment overseas, but nothing happened.”
He recently learned that a medical board at the National Institute of Ophthalmology is reviewing cases for possible overseas treatment.
“My only request is that the government gives me that opportunity,” he said.
“My only dream is to see this world with my own eyes again.”
His optimism is strengthened by the experience of another injured protester who, after treatment in Chennai, reportedly regained about half of his eyesight.
“If he can recover, maybe I can too,” Hanif said.
He acknowledged receiving Tk200,000 in government assistance and another Tk100,000 from the July Foundation.
But he said the support is insufficient for long-term treatment and rehabilitation.
Although officially recognised as a “Category A” injured July fighter, he says a promised government job for a family member has yet to materialise.
Hanif believes those who sacrificed during the uprising deserve more than financial assistance.
“Many July fighters lost their lives, their hands, their legs or their eyesight,” he said.
“They need proper treatment and rehabilitation. The families of the martyrs deserve respect. The promises made after July should also be fulfilled.”
Yet despite living with permanent disability, Hanif says he has no regrets about joining the movement.
His vision may have dimmed, but not his conviction.
“If the country ever needs me again,” he said, “I will join the movement once more. I will never step back.”

item.title: The price of July: A leg lost, a future on hold
item.description:
Nineteen-year-old Al-Amin says the hardest part of losing his leg is not the pain. It is the helplessness.
“I can’t walk. I can’t stand for long. I depend on others for almost everything,” he said.
“It is very difficult to live like this as a young man.”
Two years after the July-August uprising reshaped Bangladesh’s political landscape, Al-Amin is still waiting for the chance to rebuild the life that changed forever when a police bullet shattered his left leg.
Like many seriously injured July fighters, he says survival was only the beginning. Rehabilitation, treatment and returning to a normal life remain unfinished battles.
Al-Amin lost his left leg above the knee after being shot during the August 5 demonstrations near Brac University.
An artificial limb fitted about 18 months ago briefly allowed him to walk again. But because he was still growing, the prosthetic no longer fits.
Today, it causes such severe pain that he can barely use it.
“I could walk for about 20 minutes at first,” he recalled.
“Now the pain is unbearable whenever I wear it. I need a new artificial leg. My only hope is that the government helps us stand on our feet again.”
Before the uprising, Al-Amin was a Class X student at Dhobakhola Coronation High School in Pabna, although he lived with his family in Merul Badda, Dhaka.
Financial hardship following his injury forced him to abandon his studies.
He said he first joined demonstrations after witnessing the deadly violence around Rampura.
“The bodies of my brothers were lying on and around Rampura Bridge. I saw everything with my own eyes. After that, I could not stay at home.”
He was first injured during clashes on July 19 but returned to the streets. On August 5, another bullet pierced his left leg during demonstrations in front of Brac University.
Al-Amin alleges that instead of receiving immediate treatment, he was taken to a vaccination centre, where proper medical care was unavailable.
He further claimed police later assaulted him while he lay wounded.
“I pretended to be unconscious,” he said.
“They thought I was dead and left.”
Protesters eventually rescued him and took him to several hospitals. But he believes delays in surgery proved irreversible.
On August 10, doctors amputated his left leg about four inches above the knee.
“I have only one regret,” he said.
“If the operation had been done in time, perhaps my leg could have been saved.”
After spending nearly three months in hospital, Al-Amin returned home carrying both physical and financial burdens.
He said he received Tk100,000 in government assistance but believes the long-term support has fallen far short of what many severely injured protesters require.
He also questioned why he was classified as a “Category B” injured person despite losing an entire leg.
His childhood dream was to become a police officer.
The events of July changed that forever.
“After what I experienced, that dream disappeared.”
Now he hopes to start a small business one day.
“But I have no capital,” he said.
“I cannot even work.”
Despite everything, Al-Amin says he has never regretted joining the movement.
“I marched for my country,” he said.
“I lost a leg, but I have no regrets. I am proud that I stood for change.”
His wish today is no longer political.
It is deeply personal.
“I just want to stand on my own feet again.”

item.title: He still feels the hand he lost
item.description:
Two years after losing his right hand during the July-August uprising, 37-year-old businessman Al-Amin still wakes up feeling as though his missing fingers are moving.
Then reality returns.
“I still feel like my hand is there,” he said.
“Sometimes at night I feel my fingers moving. Then I remember I don’t have that hand anymore.”
For Al-Amin, the July uprising did not end on August 5, 2024.
It continues every day as he struggles to support his wife and three children without work, while travelling repeatedly from Mymensingh to Dhaka for medical treatment.
Like many seriously injured protesters, he says surviving the uprising was only the beginning. Rehabilitation, employment and rebuilding a normal life remain elusive.
When the anti-discrimination movement spread across the country in 2024, Al-Amin was running a small business in Mymensingh.
He said he initially watched the protests from a distance.
But the killing of Begum Rokeya University student Abu Sayed convinced him to close his shop and join the demonstrations.
“I could no longer stay at home,” he told Dhaka Tribune.
On August 5, while participating in a procession demanding the government’s resignation in Mymensingh city, he said he was attacked by Awami League activists wielding sharp weapons.
Trying to shield himself, he suffered devastating injuries.
“My right hand was severed. I was also badly injured in my head, leg and foot,” he recalled.
He believes he was specifically targeted because of his previous association with the BNP.
Fellow protesters rushed him first to Mymensingh Medical College Hospital before he was transferred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital and later the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery.
Doctors fought for more than two weeks to save his arm.
An 18-hour operation initially offered hope that it could be reattached.
But complications during subsequent surgery destroyed the remaining tissue. Even after consulting foreign specialists, doctors were unable to save the limb.
On August 22, it was amputated.
Although he later received a prosthetic hand through Brac, he says it has significant limitations.
“It works, but it is not waterproof,” he said.
“The interim government promised a better prosthetic hand from Germany. I am still waiting.”
He said he personally raised the matter with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman during a recent meeting, hoping the promise would finally be fulfilled.
Beyond the physical disability, he continues to endure chronic pain and the emotional burden of phantom limb syndrome.
“I still feel pressure in my head. Because of the metal rod in my leg, I cannot even walk properly,” he said.
Yet his memories of the uprising are not defined only by violence.
Before he was injured, he spent much of the protests distributing water and biscuits to demonstrators.
He smiled while recalling that strangers still occasionally recognise him.
“They ask me, ‘Brother, won’t you give us water? Won’t you give us biscuits?’ Hearing that makes me happy. At least I was able to do something for people.”
Financially, however, life has become increasingly difficult.
He has received Tk200,000 in government assistance, a monthly allowance of Tk20,000 and an additional Tk25,000 grant from the Prime Minister’s Office.
But he says almost all of it is consumed by treatment costs and household expenses, leaving nothing to restart his business or secure his family’s future.
“My children look at me every day,” he said quietly.
“I keep asking myself, how long can I remain unemployed?”
He says what he needs most is not charity but an opportunity to become self-reliant again.
“We are not asking for sympathy,” he said.
“We want the chance to live with dignity. If I can get a job, I can support my family and start life again.”

item.title: Notun Dhara-SDF clash halts DMCH emergency services
item.description:
Supporters of Notun Dhara Bangladesh and the State Dialogue Forum (SDF) clashed inside the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) on Tuesday night after an earlier confrontation near the Jatiya Press Club (JPC), disrupting emergency medical services.
The first clash took place around 7:00pm in front of the JPC Around 8:30pm injured members of both groups arrived at the DMCH emergency department for treatment, where fresh violence erupted.
The repeated clashes forced the emergency department to suspend services for about one and a half hours.
According to Notun Dhara Bangladesh, those injured include party Chairman Momin Mehedi, Senior Vice-Chairman Shanta Farzana, Vice-Chairman Dr Nurjahan Neera, Joint Secretary General Monir Zaman, Organising Secretary Atap Mondal and Haridas Sarkar.
The SDF said its Member Secretary ANM Ayas and several of its activists were also injured.
Shanta Farzana alleged that SDF activists, led by Ayas, attacked their torch procession and protest programme near the JPC.
She claimed that after they went to the DMCH for treatment, another group of 20 to 25 people attacked them inside the hospital, leaving several party leaders injured and trapped inside the emergency department.
On the other hand, Ayas alleged that Notun Dhara Bangladesh activists attacked SDF members after they protested remarks allegedly made about July martyr Abu Sayed and religion.
He also claimed that his supporters were targeted again after arriving at the hospital for treatment.
Meanwhile, Fahim Faruqi, central convener of Mancha-24, who also arrived at the hospital, said they would remain at the scene and cooperate with the administration while protesting what he described as offensive remarks about Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Abu Sayed and religion. He said they would avoid any aggressive behaviour.
Witnesses said panic spread through the emergency department during the clashes, forcing doctors, patients and attendants to flee for safety. Several injured people, including Shanta Farzana, Organising Secretary Atap Mondal and ANM Ayas, were seen receiving treatment.
Additional police and Ansar personnel were deployed to bring the situation under control.
DMCH Director Brig Gen Md Asaduzzaman rushed to the hospital after being informed of the incident and held a meeting with doctors in an effort to restore order.
