Turkish club Trabzonspor in 'negotiations' to sign Salah
item.description:
Mohamed Salah is in "transfer negotiations" with Trabzonspor and is expected to arrive in Turkey on Wednesday for talks, the Black Sea club said Tuesday.
The Egyptian star left Liverpool at the end of last season after an illustrious nine-year spell at Anfield, during which he won the Champions League and two Premier League titles.
"Mohamed Salah, with whom we have begun transfer negotiations, will be at Istanbul Ataturk Airport... at 12:00 on Wednesday, August 5," Trabzonspor said in a statement.
"The player is scheduled to arrive in Trabzon on the same day in the evening hours."
Salah netted 257 goals for Liverpool in 442 appearances in all competitions, making him the third top goalscorer in the club's history.
He has also scored 193 Premier League goals, 191 of them for the Reds, putting him fourth in the all-time list behind English trio Alan Shearer, Harry Kane and Wayne Rooney.
The 34-year-old Salah was far from his best in a struggling Liverpool team last term, scoring only seven times in the league.
He last played at the World Cup, helping Egypt reach the last 16 for the first time since 1934 before they blew a two-goal lead to suffer an agonising loss to eventual runners-up Argentina.
Salah had also been linked with Trabzonspor's Super Lig rivals Besiktas.
Trabzonspor finished third in the Turkish top flight last season, nine points clear of Besiktas, to qualify for the Europa League play-off round.
Salah has scored 66 goals in 119 international appearances for Egypt and is one of the most successful African players in history.

item.title: Infantino's problems mount as Wenger and key FIFA ally turn on him
item.description:
Pressure on FIFA president Gianni Infantino intensified on Tuesday, with opposition emerging from within world football's governing body as well as from external critics over his since-abandoned proposal to open the World Cup to private investment.
Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, appointed in 2019 by Infantino as FIFA's chief of global football development, said in a statement that "the decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question".
His remarks followed hot on the heels of an extraordinary internal email to FIFA staff, seen by AFP, in which secretary-general Mattias Grafstrom appeared to distance himself from Infantino on the issue.
Previously seen as close to Infantino, Grafstrom describes the fiasco surrounding the plan as "a sad and reproachable series of events".
He adds: "Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue."
FIFA had floated the plan last Tuesday, saying it could raise up to $4.2 billion based on a valuation of $20 billion for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.
By Saturday, it was dead in the water as Infantino announced the humiliating climbdown after widespread condemnation, as UEFA wielded the nuclear option of boycotting all FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.
Far from calming the waters or shoring up his presidency, Infantino has been swamped with criticism of his style of leadership and a previously smooth path to being re-elected unopposed to a fourth and final term next March in Rabat now looks a very rocky one indeed.
He has reportedly summoned FIFA staff to a crisis meeting in the Moroccan capital as he attempts to cling onto power.
Several of UEFA's member associations -- Wales, Finland, Sweden and Serbia -- have withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino and the English FA is strongly rumoured to be on the verge of also joining them.
Jordanian FA president Prince Ali bin Hussein, twice a FIFA presidential candidate, accused FIFA of "blackmail" in a remarkable statement.
Prince Ali said he was told verbally that endorsing Infantino for re-election "could go a long way to helping our FA out".
The federation had complained about not being paid for Jordan's run to last year's FIFA Arab Cup final, and about its team's fans not being given visas to watch their World Cup debut in the United States.
The Athletic also reported Tuesday that the 11 World Cup host cities in the United States are chasing up legacy payments of $1 million each which were "repeatedly" promised to them by FIFA.
- 'Take immediate steps' -
UEFA issued a letter through their lawyers in the US threatening legal action over what they had scathingly described as a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal", despite it being shelved.
Both Grafstrom and Wenger as well as chief operating officer Kevin Lamour, who had slammed the plan on Friday, are mentioned in the letter as being knowledgeable about the FFE and instructed to keep all "relevant materials".
"Dear Mr Infantino. UEFA hereby gives formal notice that it is actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints (together, the 'Proceedings') arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters as further described below," their lawyer Andrew Levander said in the letter sent last Friday and seen by AFP.
The scant comfort for Infantino came from a handful of supporters, including 2030 World Cup co-hosts Morocco, as well as Kuwait, Qatar, where he has a house, and Lebanon, which granted him honorary citizenship in February.
However, it is the damning remarks by both Wenger and Grafstrom -- who shadowed Infantino throughout the World Cup -- that will twist the knife further.
Their criticism only adds to the impression that Infantino has lost the confidence of even his closest FIFA collaborators.
One of the most devastating blows to Infantino's plan was the resignation on Friday of his special advisor Carlos Cordeiro, who is also close to US President Donald Trump.
Despite what UEFA's lawyer wrote regarding keeping material pertinent to FFE, Wenger claims to have only learned about it through the media.
"I was not involved in this strategic plan," the 76-year-old Frenchman said.
Grafstrom, for his part, tried to cheer up the staff by congratulating them on their work while admitting it had been "an extraordinary and challenging week".
For Infantino, the challenge threatens to grow, and his stated purpose when he ditched the plan, to unite football, seems unlikely to be realised while he remains president.

item.title: Pakistan close on series-levelling win against West Indies
item.description:
Pakistan's spinners put their team on course for a series-levelling victory as the West Indies stumbled to 103 for six -- a lead of just 60 runs -- on an eventful third day of the second and final Test in Trinidad on Tuesday.
Abdullah Shafique's unbeaten 160 ensured the visitors did not completely squander an excellent overnight platform in eventually getting to a first-innings total of 387.
Sajid Khan then made his second meaningful contribution of the day in taking four second-innings wickets, while Ali Usman claimed two, including home captain Roston Chase caught-and-bowled off the final ball of the day.
First-innings top-scorer Justin Greaves will carry the fight for the West Indies into the fourth morning with uncertainty over the availability to bat of regular opener Brandon King.
On a deteriorating pitch offering sharp turn and variable bounce, West Indies left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican was as much in his element as 18 months earlier against these same opponents in Multan.
Here, his haul of six for 112, including three wickets in four balls to wrap up the Pakistan innings on the stroke of tea, would have been a portent of things to come.
Yet having started the day in the comfortable position of 266 for two and within sight of the West Indies first-innings total of 344, it took an error of judgement from Pakistan captain Babar Azam to trigger a gradual slide as the visitors' last eight wickets fell for 106 runs.
Having put the West Indies bowlers to the sword with delightful, confident strokeplay on the second afternoon, Babar was a picture of strokeless paralysis at the start of the day, as if the prospect of a first Test century in almost four years had gotten the better of him.
He managed to eke out a couple of runs to add to his overnight 86 before taking off for a non-existent single and, sent back by Shafique, dived desperately but in vain as the direct hit at the striker's end by King from point found Babar short of his ground.
West Indian delight at Babar's dismissal was transformed to concern over the welfare of King, who remained prone on the outfield after effecting the dismissal.
After several minutes of assessment of his situation he was stretchered off with what was later diagnosed to be back spasms.
That unexpected breakthrough triggered a mini-slide as three wickets fell for five runs, fast bowler Shamar Joseph and Warrican claiming a wicket each.
Khan offered a measure of stability with Shafique, the pair putting on 59 for the seventh wicket before another pacer, Jayden Seales, removed the lower-order batsman for 30.
With the door open to a vulnerable tail, Warrican wasted no time in wrapping up the innings, taking three wickets in four balls with Shafique stranded at the non-striker's end and leaving Pakistan to rue opportunities missed to earn a much more significant lead.
- 'Excellent' Warrican -
Shafique's innings occupied more than seven-and-half hours during which he faced 323 deliveries, striking 15 fours and three sixes.
"Jomel was really excellent for us today, staying at the stumps and finishing off the innings well," said West Indies bowling coach Ravi Rampaul.
"At this stage though, and given the way the pitch is playing, if we can somehow push the lead to 150 we would have a chance."
Khan was at his most rampant in the final session, accounting for Tagenarine Chanderpaul and Amir Jangoo swiftly before adding Shai Hope and nightwatchman Seales to his list of victims.
Chase surveyed the carnage from the other end only to succumb to the constant pressure himself, the reaction of the home skipper to his demise almost a mirror of Babar's disconsolate trek to the pavilion more than seven hours earlier.
Usman also posed a constant threat, the left-arm spinner having earlier removed Kavem Hodge, whose 34 is the top score so far in an innings in danger of going into complete freefall.

item.title: Jordanian FA chief accuses Infantino's FIFA of 'blackmail'
item.description:
The Jordanian football association president on Tuesday accused FIFA and Gianni Infantino of attempted "blackmail" and of withholding prize money in a scathing statement.
FIFA chief Infantino has come under serious pressure over a failed plan to open the World Cup to private investment.
Prince Ali bin Hussein, who twice ran unsuccessfully for the FIFA presidency, said the Jordanian FA was still waiting to be paid for reaching last year's FIFA Arab Cup final.
He also bemoaned that several Jordan fans were not granted visas to enter the United States for the recent World Cup despite having tickets, and said Jordan's World Cup prize money is being taxed by the "US government through FIFA".
The FA's president claimed he was told that endorsing Infantino's re-election bid "would go a long way towards helping our FA out".
"We have been waiting for reward money for our players since December for the Arab Cup in Qatar, which is a FIFA event," Prince Ali, also a former FIFA vice-president, said in a statement on social media.
"The money our team should receive for having reached the final has not been delivered yet, while at the same time FIFA brags about how many billions they have in reserve.
"It is clear the problem really is with leadership.
"For months, FIFA has been refusing to help us on any of these or other matters -- until it was verbally communicated to me during the World Cup that if I endorsed Infantino it would go a long way to helping our FA out...
"We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now. But the whole situation amounts to blackmail and we refuse to give in to that."
Prince Ali lost to Sepp Blatter in the 2015 FIFA presidential election, and was then third the following year behind Infantino and Salman Bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa.
Infantino, who succeeded Blatter in 2016, was widely expected to be re-elected as FIFA president for a fourth term next March but his position is now under threat.
Earlier Tuesday, former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, FIFA's chief of global football development, and world football's governing body's secretary-general Mattias Grafstrom both criticised Infantino's handling of the scrapped investor plan.
Several of UEFA's member associations -- Wales, Finland, Sweden and Serbia -- have withdrawn their letters of support for Infantino and the English FA is strongly rumoured to be on the verge of also joining them.

item.title: Ishraque: Justice for July killings must be ensured
item.description:
State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishraque Hossain on Wednesday said the struggle will continue until those responsible for the murders during the July mass uprising are brought to justice.
He made the remarks while speaking after laying a wreath at the July Martyrs' Memorial at Shahbagh to pay tribute to those killed and injured during the July mass uprising.
“On behalf of my generation, I want to say that we have not forgotten July. We have not forgotten the July fighters. We will not stop until justice is ensured for the mass murders committed in Bangladesh,” Ishraque said.
Referring to recent developments, he said attempts were being made to create instability on campuses by forces that were on the side of the mass uprising.
The state minister alleged that the recent incidents could be part of a broader conspiracy.
“I think this could be part of a long-term conspiracy. Through this conspiracy, those from the fallen fascist regime, who looted thousands of crores of taka from Bangladesh, may try to reinvest that money to destabilise the country and eventually attempt to return,” he said.
Ishraque added that if deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina attempted to return to Bangladesh, the death sentence awarded for the mass killings must be carried out. “That will mark the end of their role in Bangladesh's politics, InshaAllah,” he said.
Calling on all to remain vigilant, he said any attempt to destabilise the country or undermine a politically and democratically elected government through unrest will be resisted.

item.title: August 5 events: Which Dhaka roads to avoid
item.description:
The Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) has issued traffic directives, urging city residents to use alternative routes and avoid certain areas in Dhaka on Wednesday, July Mass Uprising Day, to ease congestion during programmes marking the July uprising.
According to a public notice signed by DMP Commissioner Mohammad Shafiqul Islam, traffic movement around Suhrawardy Udyan, Shahbagh, Khejur Bagan and areas adjacent to Manik Mia Avenue will remain restricted from 5am on Wednesday until further notice.
U-turns and diversions will also be enforced at several points.
Mirpur Road to Farmgate via Manik Mia Avenue: Vehicles coming from the north on Mirpur Road and heading towards Farmgate or Sonargaon will turn left at Ganabhaban Crossing, take Lake Road, then turn right at the Urojahaj Crossing and Bijoy Sarani Crossing before proceeding towards Farmgate.
Farmgate to Manik Mia Avenue via Indira Road: Vehicles from Farmgate will turn right at Khejur Bagan Crossing, proceed via Urojahaj Crossing, turn left onto Lake Road and head towards Ganabhaban Crossing.
Farmgate to Shahbagh: Vehicles will turn left at Hotel InterContinental Crossing and use Hare Road and Minto Road.
Sayedabad to Shahbagh: Vehicles may travel via Mirpur Road, New Market Crossing, Azimpur Crossing, Chankharpool Crossing and Bakshibazar Crossing. Alternatively, vehicles may use Bata Crossing and Katabon Crossing, then turn towards Hatipool, Palashi and Nilkhet crossings.
Golap Shah Mazar Crossing to Shahbagh: Passenger vehicles will use the Kakrail Mosque Crossing via the High Court and Matsya Bhaban crossings.
Dhanmondi to Farmgate: Vehicles coming from Dhanmondi 27 will make a U-turn at Asad Gate-Ganabhaban Crossing, then use Lake Road, Urojahaj Crossing and Bijoy Sarani Crossing before proceeding towards Farmgate.
Asad Gate to Farmgate: Vehicles will turn left from Asad Gate, turn right at Ganabhaban Crossing and use Lake Road, Urojahaj Crossing and Bijoy Sarani Crossing to reach Farmgate.
Elevated Expressway/Indira Road to Dhanmondi: Vehicles will turn right at Khejur Bagan Crossing, proceed via Urojahaj Crossing, turn left onto Lake Road and then continue through Asad Gate towards Dhanmondi.
Mirpur Road to Dhanmondi 27: As barricades on Manik Mia Avenue will be removed, southbound vehicles from Mirpur Road will travel via Shyamoli, Shishu Mela, Ganabhaban and Asad Gate before proceeding directly towards Dhanmondi 27.
For the Dhaka Elevated Expressway, DMP has specifically requested motorists to use the FDC (Hatirjheel) ramp instead of the Farmgate exit ramp during the programs to avoid traffic congestion and inconvenience.

item.title: Bangladesh observes July Mass Uprising Day
item.description:
Bangladesh is observing July Mass Uprising Day today with nationwide programs, commemorating the student-led mass uprising that culminated in the fall of the Awami League government on August 5, 2024.
The day is being observed with state ceremonies, political programs and tributes to those killed and injured during the uprising.
The government, political parties and socio-cultural organisations have taken various programs, marking the day.
The minister, state minister, secretary, officials, and employees of the Ministry of Liberation War Affairs, along with people from different walks of life, placed wreaths at the July Martyrs' Memorial in Shahbagh on Wednesday morning.
At noon, a reception will be accorded to the families of the July martyrs and the July fighters at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in the capital. Acting President Hafiz Uddin Ahmad will attend the function as the chief guest.
Dhaka University is also observing the 2nd anniversary of the July Mass Uprising with a series of programs, including the foundation-laying of a July Memorial and a dedicated July Corner in the university's Central Library.
A discussion on the July uprising will be held at the TSC where five families of the July martyrs will be honoured, and a prayer session will be held after Asr prayers at the Central Mosque, seeking eternal peace for the martyrs.
Bangladesh missions abroad also chalked out discussion programs on the occasion.
Religious institutions across the country are organising special munajat and prayers.
Meanwhile, acting President Hafiz Uddin Ahmad and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman issued separate messages on the occasion of July Mass Uprising Day.
In his message, Hafiz Uddin Ahmad extended his heartfelt greetings and congratulations to the valiant July warriors and all patriotic citizens of the country, saying the nation will forever remember their extraordinary sacrifices, boundless courage and outstanding contributions as an enduring source of inspiration.
He also called for upholding the dignity of the martyrs’ sacrifices, building a humane Bangladesh that belongs to the people, where fascist and authoritarian rule, as well as extremism, will never again find a place.
The acting president urged all to unite in building a new Bangladesh that is democratic, just, humane, free from discrimination, happy and prosperous and work together to realise the dreams, ideals, hopes and aspirations of the martyrs who made the supreme sacrifice in the Great War of Independence and the July Mass Uprising.
In his message, the prime minister described August 5 as a day of joy, a day of victory and a day of the restoration of democratic political rights for all those who cherish freedom and democracy.
He said for more than one and a half decades, in the struggle against fascism and for the restoration of the people's right to vote and their democratic rights, the BNP, other anti-fascist political parties, and the people of differing views had to endure limitless persecution and repression.
Tarique Rahman said countless people became victims of enforced disappearance, murder, abduction, assaults, false cases, torture and oppression. “In leading this movement, the uncompromising leader of the nation, former Prime Minister late Begum Khaleda Zia, was also forced to spend years in the prison of the oppressors on false charges.”
He remembered with profound respect all the martyrs. “By sacrificing their lives for the freedom, rights and dignity of the country and its people, they have left us in their debt. Bangladesh owes an enduring debt to every martyr's family. Now it is our turn to repay that debt.”
The prime minister urged all to make a pledge to honour that debt through sincere efforts to build a just, self-reliant, democratic and humane Bangladesh by ensuring the political and economic empowerment of people and by establishing equality, human dignity and social justice.
Meanwhile, Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) has taken extensive and multi-layered security measures to maintain law and order and ensure public safety in the capital ahead of July Mass Uprising Day.
The measures have been taken to prevent any act of sabotage, untoward incident or disruption to public safety during the observance of the day, according to a DMP statement issued on Tuesday.
As part of the security plan, the number of police patrols and checkpoints has been significantly increased across the capital, with stricter search operations at all entry points to Dhaka.
On June 26, 2025, the government declared August 5 as July Mass Uprising Day. The day is a public holiday.

item.title: Teesta flows 13cm above danger level in Lalmonirhat
item.description:
The Teesta River was flowing 13 centimetres above the danger level at the Dalia point of the Teesta Barrage in Nilphamari on Wednesday morning as continuous rainfall and upstream hill runoff caused the water level to rise sharply.
Shunil Kumar, executive engineer of the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) in Lalmonirhat, said the water level was recorded at 9am.
As the river continued to swell, water began entering low-lying houses and agricultural land along its banks, he said.
However, no major financial losses are expected as there are currently no significant seasonal crops in the affected fields, the official said.
The BWDB said water levels in rivers across the northern region may continue to rise over the next 48 hours due to heavy rainfall and upstream inflows, potentially triggering minor flooding in low-lying areas.
All necessary preparations have been taken to respond to any flood-related situation, it said.

item.title: 52 tons of green chillis imported from India in two days
item.description:
Bangladesh imported nearly 52 tons of green chillies from India through the Benapole land port in two days amid a sharp rise in prices in the local markets.
On Tuesday evening, three Indian trucks carrying 42,220kg of green chillies entered the port. Another 9,200kg arrived on Monday, taking the two-day total to 51,420kg.
The consignments were cleared and sent to different parts of the country soon after completing port formalities. Shimu Enterprise imported the chillies, with Shimu Shipping Lines acting as the C&F agent.

What happens to fugitive dictators?
item.description:
An inevitable yet unforeseen event occurred two years ago on 5 August 2024—the fall and escape of the autocratic ruler Sheikh Hasina. For almost 16 years, the accumulated anger of the oppressed and persecuted people of Bangladesh erupted in a 35-day movement before this.

When the people overcome the fear of an autocrat's oppression, the fall of that ruler becomes inevitable; Bangladesh had reached that point even before 5 August. Therefore, 5 August was just the final episode. Hasina's escape was, in a sense, inevitable. Dictators around the world flee in the face of public outrage. Sheikh Hasina used to boast, "Sheikh Hasina or the Awami League never runs away, has never run away."

It has been two years since Hasina’s escape. Meanwhile, in absentia, she has been sentenced to death in a case for crimes against humanity. Currently, she is in India under asylum. She appears on social media and speaks to foreign journalists. But what might her future hold? Perhaps, the fate of ousted rulers in different countries might provide some insight into what the future may hold for Sheikh Hasina.

Passing away in privacy

Dictators who are unable to leave the country in the face of public uprisings or try to resist with their supporters, often face brutal assassination. The history of Libya's Muammar Gaddafi dates back to 2011; in 1989, Nicolae Ceausescu of Romania, trying to escape with his wife during an uprising, was caught by protesters and they were killed.

Those who managed to take refuge in other countries, some ended quietly, out of the public eye. After the Islamic Revolution of Iran in 1979, the fugitive Reza Shah Pahlavi, while seeking refuge across six countries in just a year and a half, died in Cairo in poor health. Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines, after ruling the country for 20 years, was ousted in 1986 and took refuge in Hawaii, United States, where he died in 1989.

In 1990, Chad’s president Hissène Habré was overthrown by a military coup and fled to Senegal, where he died in 2021. The ruler of Tunisia, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, after facing a public uprising in 2011, took refuge in Saudi Arabia, where he died in 2019. Although they managed to draw the world's attention during their rule, the news of their deaths barely gained significance, with many even unaware of their obsequies.

Inactive life

A large number of fugitive rulers, upon finding asylum in other countries, effectively retire from political life and lead inactive lives in obscurity. Bashar al-Assad of Syria, after being removed from power, took refuge in Russia in December 2024, but since then, nothing has been known about his situation, nor any statements made by him.

The same happened with Afghanistan’s President Ashraf Ghani. When the Taliban took Kabul, he fled to the United Arab Emirates in August 2021. In Ukraine, a mass uprising took place in February 2014; President Viktor Yanukovych fled the country to Russia. It has been said that he lived in the city of Rostov.

However, an investigative report in July this year revealed that he is living in Sochi under an assumed name. It is believed that host countries, for diplomatic reasons, provide asylum to the fugitives under this condition.

Whether these defeated, devastated, and virtually isolated former rulers are interested in returning to politics is also a question. Furthermore, they seem to prefer enjoying a lavish lifestyle funded by the extensive wealth acquired through corruption during their time in power.

Extradition

In most cases, efforts are made to bring these fugitive rulers back to face trial in their home country, but with little success. In 1991, when the backdrop of civil war in Ethiopia caused ruler Mengistu Haile Mariam to flee to Zimbabwe, he was granted political asylum there.

Though the Ethiopian government requested his extradition, Zimbabwe’s government did not comply. After Robert Mugabe's fall from power in Zimbabwe, there were indications that Haile Mariam would be extradited, but this never happened.

In 2000, Peru’s ruler Alberto Fujimori fled to Japan for asylum. Although Peru’s government requested Japan for extradition, it was denied citing his dual Japanese citizenship. However, Fujimori voluntarily traveled to Chile in 2005, where he was detained based on an international warrant issued by the Peruvian government. In 2007, Chile extradited him to Peru.

Kyrgyz President Kurmanbek Bakiyev fled to Belarus in 2010. The Kyrgyz government has been demanding Bakiyev’s extradition since then, but Belarus has not complied; Bakiyev remains there under official hospitality.

Trial

The trial of fugitives in absentia in their home country is generally considered normal. In Ethiopia, the trial against Mengistu Haile Mariam for various crimes, including genocide, started in 1994. At the end of this trial in 2006, the court sentenced him to life imprisonment. In a high court appeal ruling in 2008, his life sentence was increased to a death sentence.

In 2012, Tunisia’s court tried former ruler Ben Ali and his wife in multiple cases, sentencing them to life, 35 years, and 20 years in prison.

Kyrgyzstan's fugitive head of state, Kurmanbek Bakiyev, was sentenced to life imprisonment for his involvement in the killing of protesters during the 2010 uprising.

In 2014, after having to flee to Ivory Coast following a mass uprising, Burkina Faso’s President Blaise Compaoré was found guilty by the country’s court in 2022 for the assassination of his predecessor and sentenced to life imprisonment. Blaise Compaoré has since acquired Ivorian citizenship.

Although not tried in Chad, the trial of President Hissène Habré took place in Senegal, where he had taken refuge. Following persistent efforts by the victims, he was arrested in Senegal in 2013. In 2016, a special court supported by the African union in Senegal found him guilty of war crimes, crimes against humanity, and torture, sentencing him to life imprisonment.

This trial and conviction were the first instance where a former head of state was tried for human rights violations in a court of a country or regional organisation. In Ukraine, former President Viktor Yanukovych was sentenced to 13 years imprisonment on charges of treason by a domestic court in 2019, and another 15 years in 2025 in a separate case.

There are instances of former dictators being tried in person in their home country. Erich Honecker, the head of East Germany, was tried after unification in Germany. After falling from power, a summons against Honecker was issued in 1991, leading him to flee to Moscow in December. He sought refuge in the Chilean embassy and applied for Soviet citizenship. Though he wished to go to Chile, the Chilean government did not agree.

On 29 July 1992, he was forcibly evicted from the Chilean embassy and flown to Berlin. He was arrested at the airport. Meanwhile, charges were framed against him, and his trial with other accused started in November 1992. It became known that he was suffering from cancer and was not expected to live beyond six months. His lawyers appealed for his release on humanitarian grounds. After initially rejecting the appeal, it was accepted. Honecker was released in January 1993 and went to Chile to be with his family, where he died in May 1994.

An example of domestic trial and sentencing is that of Peru's ruler Fujimori. After being extradited from Chile in 2007, he faced trial. In 2009, the Peruvian court sentenced him to 25 years in prison. Although he was released by the Peruvian president in 2017 on humanitarian grounds due to deteriorating health, the court overturned the pardon, sending him back to prison. In December 2023, Peru’s Constitutional Court upheld the presidential pardon. Released from prison, Fujimori died in September 2024.

Return

The return of fugitives to their home country is rare. A recent example is Gotabaya Rajapaksa of Sri Lanka. In July 2022, amid widespread protests, he left the country for the Maldives, staying briefly in Singapore and Thailand. He returned to the country after just 55 days. Leaders of the then-ruling party welcomed him at the airport.

Multiple lawsuits have been filed against Rajapaksa, including one linked to the 2019 Easter bombings at three churches that killed 270 people. It was alleged his government was involved, and he was aware. In June, a court imposed a travel ban on him.

Another notable example is Ali Abdullah Saleh of Yemen. During the 2011 uprising, after an assassination attempt left him injured, he went to Saudi Arabia ‘for treatment’. But in efforts to cling to power, he returned to the country in a few months. Failing to control the situation, he transferred power and stayed in the United States temporarily.

However, after 2014, he formed an alliance with the rebel Houthi faction and actively engaged in military operations against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. In 2017, a dispute with the Houthi faction arose, leading to his assassination by the Houthis.

None of these outcomes for dictators were predetermined. There was no guarantee these events would unfold exactly the way they did. However, at some point, fugitive autocrats have to accept that they are removed from the political scene; there are examples where attempts to change this have not ended well.

item.title: PM: Justice for anti-fascist movement killings to be transparent, impartial
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday said those responsible for the killings during the anti-fascist movement will be brought to justice through transparent, impartial and credible trials conducted in accordance with the due process of law. “The killers in the anti-fascist movement will be tried in a transparent, impartial and credible manner following the due process of law. The government believes justice for every crime is essential to ensure the rule of law,” he added. The prime minister made the remarks while addressing a discussion titled "July-36" after inaugurating the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum at Ganabhaban in the capital’s Sher-e-Bangla Nagar. Tarique Rahman said the government has decided to name institutions after those killed or became victims of enforced disappearance and other violence over the past 17 years and during the July Mass Uprising. “The government has decided to name an institution in the respective localities after every person who embraced martyrdom or became a victim of enforced disappearance and killing during the past 17 years and the July movement,” he said. Speaking about the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum, the prime minister said the country’s democratic people expect the museum not to become a place for promoting the exclusive political narrative of any individual, group or political party. “The 2024 mass uprising did not belong to any individual, group or political party. The true heroes of the uprising are the democratic people of Bangladesh,” he said. Tarique Rahman said the 1971 Liberation War was fought to achieve the country’s independence, while the 2024 mass uprising was waged to safeguard the independence of the state and the freedom of its people. “Just as the people have never forgotten the freedom fighters of 1971, they will never forget those who laid down their lives in 2024 to protect the country and the freedom of its people,” he said.
Warning against attempts to create instability in the country, the Prime Minister urged all concerned to avoid creating unnecessary controversies. “I urge everyone to reflect on whether, by creating unnecessary issues and such situations in a fascism-free Bangladesh, they are unknowingly paving the way for the resurgence of ousted and fugitive autocratic forces,” he said. Recalling authoritarian rule of more than one and a half decades, Tarique Rahman said the country had paid a heavy price in its struggle for democracy. He said: “Today marks another milestone in Bangladesh’s democratic history. During more than one and a half decades of the anti-fascist movement, thousands of people became victims of enforced disappearance and abduction. “Millions suffered repression, persecution, attacks and false cases, forcing them to remain away from their homes for years,” he said, adding: “During the July-August Mass Uprising alone, thousands of students, people from all walks of life, women and children embraced martyrdom.” The prime minister said: “The fascist forces even opened fire from helicopters during the July-August Mass Uprising and killed pro-democracy people.” Such cruelty and brutality by the fallen, defeated and ousted fascist forces are rare in the civilised world, the premier said, adding: “During the fascist regime, enforced disappearances, killings and abductions were turned into a matter of routine.” “The brutality that persisted for more than one and a half decades can only be compared to the three-and-a-half years of misrule under the Awami League government after independence,” said the prime minister.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman addresses the discussion titled ‘July-36’ after inaugurating the July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum in Dhaka on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. Photo: PMO Referring to the role of the historic July Mass Uprising Memorial Museum, the prime minister said it would preserve the courageous legacy of the nation’s predecessors for future generations. “This museum will also unveil the true face of the ousted fascist forces to the new generation,” he said. Tarique Rahman said: “This memorial museum is a historic initiative to permanently preserve in our national memory the struggles, sacrifices, suffering, courage and democratic aspirations of our people. “I hope it will not remain only a memorial to the tragic events of 2024. It will also present the relationship between the July Mass Uprising and Bangladesh's broader democratic journey,” he said. “Not only the history of the July Mass Uprising, but also the history of every democratic movement and struggle in Bangladesh should be preserved here,” added the prime minister. Stating that the ousted fascist forces had never been able to accept democratic rule, the prime minister said their predecessors had buried democracy by amending the Constitution in 1975. “Later, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, the declarer of Bangladesh's independence, restored multi-party democracy after assuming the responsibility of running the state,” he said, adding: “Future generations will certainly benefit if these chapters of history are also preserved at the museum,” he said. The prime minister underscored the importance of preserving history with accuracy, saying: “Incomplete, exaggerated or motivated narratives do not strengthen history. Rather, they undermine its credibility and create grounds for future divisions.” “Therefore, factual accuracy should be ensured in every matter. At the same time, presenting the museum's exhibits in English and other languages alongside Bangla will help people from different linguistic backgrounds learn about Bangladesh’s democratic struggles,” he said.
Regarding the rehabilitation and treatment of the injured July fighters, Tarique Rahman said the government has been providing them with free medical treatment at public hospitals. “At the same time, those who sustained serious injuries are being sent for advanced treatment in Thailand, Singapore, Türkiye, Russia and other countries in accordance with the prescribed procedures,” he said. He said 50 July fighters are currently undergoing treatment abroad. “More than 13,000 gazetted July fighters are receiving monthly honorarium allowances, based on their respective categories, directly through their own bank accounts,” he added. The prime minister also said the present government is sincere in extending state support to those who were killed or injured during the anti-fascist movement. Reaffirming his government’s commitment to state reform, Tarique Rahman said in addition to providing financial support to the July fighters, the present government has begun the work of building the Bangladesh envisioned by the martyrs. “As part of that effort, implementation of the 31-point election manifesto, as well as the July Charter signed at the South Plaza of the National Parliament, has begun in phases with the goal of rebuilding the country,” he said. He said the Special Committee on Constitutional Amendment, formed in parliament, had also started its work to fulfil the aspiration for the referendum. “By rebuilding the country, we will, InShaAllha, establish a self-reliant, prosperous, secure and democratic Bangladesh—the Bangladesh envisioned by the martyrs,” he said. At the conclusion of his speech, the prime minister congratulated the Bangladesh Army for standing by the people during the mass uprising and expressed deep condolences to the bereaved families of the martyrs. “Bangladesh will never again become a subservient state,” he asserted. The discussion was followed by a cultural program featuring patriotic songs, recitations and performances by eminent artistes, highlighting the spirit of the July Mass Uprising, patriotism and democratic values. The program began with the playing of the national anthem, followed by recitations from the Holy Quran and other religious scriptures. Former interim government chief adviser Prof Muhammad Yunus attended the program as a special guest. Family members of several July uprising martyrs, including the mothers of Shariar Khan Anas and Abdullah Bin Jahid, as well as July warrior Tabassum Prapti, shared their memories and reflections during the event. Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Azam Khan, State Minister Ali Newaz Mahmood Khyom, Prime Minister's Adviser on Information and Cultural Affairs Zahed Ur Rahman, and Cultural Affairs Secretary Kaniz Moula addressed the program. LGRD and Co-operatives Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood, State Minister for Civil Aviation and Tourism M Rashiduzzaman Millat, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam, Prime Minister's Office Spokesperson Mahdi Amin, the Prime Minister's daughter Barrister Zaima Rahman, Press Secretary AAM Saleh Shibly, Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon, diplomats, members of civil society, eminent citizens, families of the July martyrs, injured July warriors, and senior government officials were present at the programme.

item.title: Acting President: Supporting July martyrs' families govt's sacred duty
item.description:
Acting President Hafiz Uddin Ahmad Bir Bikram on Wednesday said ensuring the welfare of the families of those martyred in the July Mass Uprising, along with the treatment and rehabilitation of the injured, is the present government's most important and sacred responsibility.
"The most important task of this government is to look after the families of those who made the supreme sacrifice in the July movement. This is our most sacred responsibility. It is also the government's sacred duty to provide treatment and rehabilitation to those who were injured or lost their eyesight or limbs," he said.
He made the remarks while addressing a reception and discussion for the families of the July martyrs and July fighters as the chief guest at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre, marking July Mass Uprising Day 2026.
Describing the day as one inscribed in "golden letters" in the nation's history, Hafiz Uddin said it marked the victory of freedom-loving students and people who cherish democracy, justice and human dignity.
He said the mass uprising in July 2024 brought an end to prolonged autocratic and fascist rule, forcing those associated with the government to flee the country and opening a new chapter for Bangladesh.
The acting president paid profound tribute to the martyrs of the July Mass Uprising, including Abu Sayeed, Mugdha, Wasim, Yamin, Farhan, Nafiz, Sajal, Rabbi, Meraj, Elem, Taim, Naima, little child Riya Gope and Ahad, and prayed for the eternal peace of their souls. He said their sacrifices and patriotism would continue to inspire the nation.
Recalling the presence of a mother and her son who lost his eyesight during the movement, Hafiz Uddin said the sight deeply moved him.
"The young man lost his eyesight in the struggle to restore democracy and establish the rule of law. If they are not accorded due dignity and have to go from minister to minister even for their modest needs, it would be a matter of shame for the nation," he said.
Addressing the July fighters and the families of the martyrs, he said they should not lose hope, assuring them that the government would honor their sacrifices and do everything within its capacity for their welfare.
"I want to assure you that if this elected government makes any mistakes, you will bring them to our attention and we will correct ourselves," he said.
Referring to the Awami League, Hafiz Uddin said: "We are not like the Awami League and we do not want to be like them. Look at the Awami League; they have no remorse. Despite so much injustice, oppression, killings, enforced disappearances, money laundering, murder, torture and Aynaghar, they feel no shame."
He also referred to remarks about the party's possible return to the country.
"They again say they will return to the country in December. We are waiting. Come, return to the country. Inshallah, we will meet on the streets," he said.
Recalling his role in the 1971 Liberation War, Hafiz Uddin said: "I fought in the Liberation War at the age of 27. Now, at the age of 82, I will fight another one for Bangladesh and its people, to make good governance and democracy permanent."
He said few nations in the world have citizens who can stand before raised guns with both hands lifted like Abu Sayeed, adding that Bangladesh should take pride in such courage.
The Acting President said the July Mass Uprising had created an opportunity to rebuild the state, stressing that the national goal should now be to establish a democratic, justice-based and corruption-free Bangladesh where every citizen enjoys equal rights and dignity.
"Today we stand at the beginning of a new journey. This journey will not be easy. Differences of opinion will remain, but on issues of national interest, democratic values, and the country's independence and sovereignty, we must demonstrate unity, restraint and wisdom," he said.
He urged the nation to remain vigilant so that division, hatred and narrow interests do not obstruct national progress.
Calling on people to embrace the spirit of the July Mass Uprising, Hafiz Uddin urged citizens to strengthen unity, patriotism, honesty and mutual respect.
"Let us transform this new possibility, earned through the blood of the martyrs, into a firm commitment to build a new Bangladesh free from discrimination," he said.
Drawing a parallel between the Liberation War and the July Mass Uprising, he said both movements were fought to establish democracy.
Concluding his speech, the Acting President called upon every citizen to remain vigilant in safeguarding the dignity of Bangladesh.
Earlier, Hafiz Uddin presented crests to representatives of the families of the July martyrs and the July fighters.
The event was chaired by Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Aazam Khan. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed and State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishraque Hossain attended as special guests, while representatives of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, the National Citizens Committee and senior government officials were also present.
Secretary of the Ministry of Liberation War Affairs Md Ashraful Islam delivered the welcome address, while representatives of the families of the July martyrs and the July fighters shared their experiences and expectations.
The program began with the national anthem and recitations from the holy scriptures. A one-minute silence was observed in memory of the July martyrs, followed by the screening of a documentary on the July Mass Uprising.

item.title: Jamaat ameer: Another revolution imminent, people must prepare
item.description:
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer and Opposition Leader in Parliament Dr Shafiqur Rahman on Wednesday said that "another revolution" appears to be imminent, calling on the people to prepare for what he described as the next phase of the movement against fascism.
Speaking as the chief guest at a rally organized by the 11-party alliance at the south gate of Baitul Mukarram National Mosque, marking the second anniversary of the July Mass Uprising, Shafiqur alleged that the country was again heading toward a situation that would require public resistance.
Addressing unnamed political opponents, he said that if they had not "betrayed" the people, there would have been no reason for unrest, adding that his party could not remain silent while the country faced its current circumstances.
He said revolutions transcend age, noting that people of all ages had participated in the July Mass Uprising and expressing hope that they would again take part in future movements. He also said the struggle against what he described as fascism would continue.
Shafiqur said threats of imprisonment, repression or execution would not deter his party, adding that, if necessary, they would embrace even the gallows in pursuit of what they believe is the nation's liberation.
Claiming that some political actors who had once been victims of oppression were now repeating the same practices, the Jamaat chief urged them to refrain from what he called fascist behavior. He said that if leaders respected the people, they would, in turn, earn public respect, while vowing that no form of fascism would be tolerated in Bangladesh.
He also urged the government to respect what he described as the people's mandate, claiming that ignoring public opinion had historically led to the downfall of those in power.
Shafiqur further alleged that his party was facing continuous pressure to compromise and being offered various inducements, but said Jamaat would continue to safeguard the people's mandate and would not retreat from its demands under any circumstances.
Referring to recent developments on university campuses, he claimed that students and teachers were living in fear and alleged that the culture of "gonorooms" and "guest rooms" was re-emerging. He called on students, teachers and staff to resist injustice wherever it occurs.
Criticizing the recent increase in gas prices, the Jamaat ameer alleged that authorities first create an artificial gas shortage before raising prices and then resolve the crisis afterward. He described the practice as deception against the public.
The rally was chaired by Bangladesh Khelafat Majlish Ameer Mamunul Haque and was also addressed by other leaders of the 11-party alliance.

item.title: 10 injured in clash between Chhatra Dal, Shibir activists at Barisal University
item.description:
At least 10 people were injured in a clash between activists of Chhatra Dal and Chhatra Shibir at Barisal University on Wednesday over allegations that outsiders had joined a campus rally.
The clash broke out in the morning when the university unit of Chhatra Shibir brought out a procession titled "Indomitable July," according to witnesses and campus sources.
An argument reportedly began after Chhatra Dal activists objected to the alleged presence of outsiders in the rally. The altercation later escalated into a clash, followed by several rounds of chase and counter-chase.
Ashiq Ahmed, senior vice-president of the university unit of Chhatra Dal, alleged that Chhatra Shibir had entered the campus with outsiders carrying sticks and flags.
He claimed that Shibir activists attacked Chhatra Dal members after they requested that the programme be held without outsiders, leaving five to six of their activists injured.
Rejecting the allegation, Zakaria Islam Babu, general secretary of the university unit of Chhatra Shibir, said they had been holding a peaceful program marking the anniversary of the July Uprising when Chhatra Dal activists attacked them near the vice-chancellor's gate.
He claimed that around five Shibir activists were injured in the attack and alleged that the incident occurred in the presence of university authorities. Although the university proctor tried to control the situation, the attack continued, he added.
Zakaria also said a complaint had been submitted to the university's vice-chancellor seeking justice over the incident.
Both student organisations blamed each other for triggering the violence.
The university proctor could not be reached for comment.
Belal Hossain, additional deputy commissioner of Barisal Metropolitan Police, said police rushed to the campus after receiving information about the clash.
"Additional police have been deployed on the campus following the incident. We have urged both sides to remain calm," he said.
Earlier on Tuesday, violence erupted as activists of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) and Bangladesh Islami Chhatra Shibir clashed at several educational institutions in the capital, leaving dozens injured.

item.title: State July celebration disrupted over documentary controversy
item.description:
A state ceremony marking the second anniversary of the July Mass Uprising descended into protests on Wednesday after audience members accused the government of distorting the movement’s history through an official documentary, forcing ministers to apologise and promise immediate corrections.
The unprecedented disruption unfolded in the presence of Acting President Hafiz Uddin Ahmed Bir Bikram at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Center, where families of July martyrs, injured protesters, students and political activists interrupted the program with chants of “Fake, fake” after the documentary was screened.
The protest briefly threw the nationally televised event into disorder, prompting members of the acting president’s security detail to take positions on the stage and inside the auditorium while several invited foreign guests left the venue amid the commotion.
The controversy centred on allegations that the documentary failed to accurately portray the July uprising, omitted key developments -- particularly the events of August 3 -- and inadequately reflected the sacrifices of protesters and the movement’s leadership.
As slogans echoed through the auditorium, organisers repeatedly appealed for calm, but the protest continued.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed eventually addressed the gathering, inviting protesters to speak from the stage and urging them to remain seated.
Seeking to defuse tensions, he requested National Citizen Party (NCP) Member Secretary Akhtar Hossain to address the audience.
Akhtar acknowledged the concerns raised by protesters, saying the documentary contained “inconsistencies” that required correction.
“We have also seen the inconsistencies in the documentary,” he said.
“The events of August 3 are completely absent. We will raise these issues with the government and seek accountability from the ministry. But on this historic day, we must remain calm out of respect for the families of the martyrs.”
Following his appeal, Akhtar and other NCP leaders left the venue after taking permission from the acting president.
As protests continued, Liberation War Affairs Minister Ahmed Aazam Khan returned to the stage and publicly apologised to the audience.
“Today’s documentary has caused you pain,” he said.
“The July movement and the mass uprising belong to all of us. We will carefully review every inconsistency, including the omission of the events of August 3, and take immediate steps to correct them.”
He also assured the audience that the documentary would be reviewed in consultation with representatives of the martyrs’ families and injured July fighters before being revised.
Only after the minister’s apology and commitment to amend the film did the protesters withdraw their objections, allowing the remainder of the program to proceed.
The event, organised by the Ministry of Liberation War Affairs, began with a reception for the families of July martyrs and injured July fighters before the documentary was shown.

item.title: Swapon calls for equitable, accountable state inspired by July Uprising
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon on Wednesday called on all to work together to build an equitable, accountable and humane state inspired by the spirit of the July Mass Uprising.
Speaking at a discussion and reception for families of the July martyrs at the District Shilpakala Academy auditorium in Barishal, organized to mark July Mass Uprising Day 2026, the minister said the ideals of the historic movement must remain alive in the hearts of every citizen.
He said the spirit forged through the sacrifices and aspirations of thousands of people must not be undermined by any force, urging everyone to remain united and vigilant.
Swapon said that a group and a single family had monopolised democracy and people's rights for years, weakening democratic institutions and depriving citizens of their voting rights.
He urged people from all walks of life, regardless of political affiliation, religion or ethnicity, to forge unity to protect democracy.
The minister said attempts had been made to divide people through intimidation, greed and promises of power, but conscious citizens rejected such temptations and prioritised the country's interests.
He emphasized that the July Mass Uprising was not the work of a few individuals but a collective resistance against prolonged deprivation, injustice and oppression.
The strength of this movement is laying in the unity, courage and unwavering faith of the people in democracy, he said.
Barisal Divisional Commissioner Khalil Ahmed chaired the program, where government officials, political leaders, media representatives and families of the July martyrs were present.
A documentary on the July martyrs was also screened.

item.title: 5 protein-rich seeds to add to your diet
item.description:
Protein plays a vital role in building and repairing muscles, producing hormones and enzymes, healing tissues, and supporting healthy skin, hair, and blood. While meat, fish, eggs, and dairy are well-known protein sources, several seeds also provide a significant amount of plant-based protein, along with fiber, healthy fats, vitamins, and minerals.
Here are five protein-rich seeds worth adding to your diet:
Pumpkin seeds
Pumpkin seeds are among the richest plant-based sources of protein. A 28-gram serving (about one ounce) provides around 7 grams of protein. They are also rich in fiber, magnesium, zinc, and essential amino acids, including tryptophan, making them a nutritious snack or salad topping.
Chia seeds
Just two tablespoons of chia seeds provide about 5 grams of protein. They also contain fiber, omega-3 fatty acids, and essential amino acids that support muscle recovery and tissue repair. Their combination of protein, fiber, and healthy fats may help promote fullness, support healthy weight management, and maintain steady blood sugar levels. Chia seeds are also a good source of calcium and phosphorus, which help support bone health.
Flaxseeds
Two tablespoons of flaxseeds contain approximately 5-6 grams of protein. They are also rich in fiber and plant-based omega-3 fatty acids. Regular consumption may help support heart health, improve digestion, and contribute to healthy cholesterol levels as part of a balanced diet.
Sunflower seeds
A 28-gram serving of sunflower seeds provides about 6 grams of protein. They are also an excellent source of vitamin E, magnesium, and selenium. Their protein and amino acid content supports muscle maintenance and tissue repair, making them a nutritious post-workout snack.
Sesame seeds
Three tablespoons of sesame seeds contain roughly 5 grams of protein. They provide essential amino acids, including methionine, which plays a role in protein synthesis and tissue repair. Rich in calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, sesame seeds also help support bone health and overall nutrition.

item.title: Sand-laden trucks outside Khaleda Zia's residence: Ex-joint secretary sent to jail
item.description:
A Dhaka court on Wednesday sent former joint secretary Syed Jaglul Pasha to jail in a case over allegations that he helped obstruct former prime minister Khaleda Zia from attending a political rally in 2013 by barricading the road outside her Gulshan residence with sand-laden trucks and using pepper spray.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Kamal Uddin passed the order after Gulshan Zonal Team Inspector Anwar Hossain produced Jaglul Pasha before the court and sought a 10-day remand. The court fixed Thursday for the remand hearing. SI Mokhtar Hossain of the prosecution confirmed the matter
Jaglul was arrested by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police's Detective Branch (DB) from his Bashundhara residence at around 1:30am on Tuesday.
According to the case statement, Jaglul was among 111 named accused, along with 250-300 unidentified individuals, who allegedly gathered outside Khaleda Zia's Gulshan residence on December 28, 2013, armed with deadly weapons. They allegedly remained there throughout the day, assaulted BNP leaders and activists, carried out acts of sabotage by blocking roads, and created obstacles to prevent Khaleda Zia from attending a scheduled political rally.
The complaint further alleged that at around 9am on December 29, 2013, when Khaleda Zia was preparing to leave for the rally with her entourage, the accused barricaded the road with sand-laden trucks and other vehicles. Despite repeated attempts to leave, they allegedly prevented her movement and used banned pepper spray with the intent to kill, leaving Khaleda Zia and several leaders and activists accompanying her injured.
The case was filed at Gulshan Police Station in October 2024 by Shariful Islam Shawon, former joint secretary of the Latif Hall unit of Rajshahi University Chhatra Dal.
Jaglul Pasha also faces allegations in the Zia Orphanage Trust case of preparing forged documents and giving false testimony before the court in proceedings involving former prime minister Khaleda Zia.

item.title: Three everyday kitchen items that could be harming your health
item.description:
Some everyday kitchen items—including old sponges, damaged non-stick pans, and dishwashing liquids with harsh chemicals—can pose hidden health risks if they are not used or replaced properly. Experts say simple changes in your kitchen routine can help reduce the risk of foodborne illness and unnecessary chemical exposure.
Old kitchen sponge
Kitchen sponges stay damp for long periods, making them an ideal breeding ground for bacteria and fungi. Over time, they can harbor harmful bacteria such as Salmonella and E. coli . These microbes can contaminate dishes and food, increasing the risk of foodborne illness, including diarrhea, vomiting, stomach infections, and fever.
When to replace it:
Dishwashing liquid with harsh chemicals
Some dishwashing liquids contain artificial fragrances, dyes, and other chemicals that may cause irritation in sensitive individuals. If dishes are not rinsed thoroughly, small amounts of residue may remain on the surface. In some people, this may contribute to skin irritation, dermatitis, eye irritation, or respiratory discomfort.
How to use it safely:
Damaged non-stick pan
A non-stick pan with deep scratches or a peeling coating should be replaced. Tiny particles from the damaged coating may end up in food, while overheating worn non-stick cookware can release fumes that may irritate the eyes and throat and cause temporary flu-like symptoms known as polymer fume fever.
Experts also recommend avoiding overheating non-stick cookware and considering alternatives such as stainless steel, cast iron, or tri-ply cookware.
Safe cookware practices:
Small changes can make a big difference
These kitchen items are not inherently dangerous, but improper use or failure to replace them regularly can increase health risks. Simple habits—such as replacing your sponge regularly, choosing gentler cleaning products, and discarding damaged cookware—can help reduce the risk of foodborne illness and unnecessary exposure to potentially harmful substances.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 854 as five die in 24 hours
item.description:
Five more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Wednesday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 854.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all five of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 758, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 96, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the five new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with three deaths reported in both the Dhaka division and Dhaka district.
A total of 959 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Wednesday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 132,905.
During the same period, 124 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 16,655.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 115,234 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 111,005 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: Dengue: 195 cases recorded in 24 hours
item.description:
Health officials on Wednesday said they recorded 195 fresh cases of dengue onslaughts in the past 24 hours.
“During the period, (of the 195) 15 patients were hospitalized in Barisal division, 77 in Chittagong division, 21 in Dhaka division, 34 in Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) and 26 in Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) areas, 10 in Khulna division and 12 in Rangpur division, a Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) statement said.
Since the start of the dengue onslaughts, Bangladesh this year has witnessed so far 59 deaths while the disease inflicted 17,409.
Last year, dengue claimed 413 lives and inflicted 1,02,861 people in the country.
Besides, dengue claimed 575 lives and inflicted 1,01,214 people in 2024.

item.title: Rubaiyat Hossain's ‘The Difficult Bride’ selected for 51st Toronto Film Festival
item.description:
National Film Award-winning filmmaker Rubaiyat Hossain's latest feature, The Difficult Bride, has been selected for the 51st Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), marking another international milestone after becoming the first Bangladeshi feature film chosen for the Orizzonti section of the 83rd Venice International Film Festival.
Rubaiyat shared the news on social media, writing: "Next stop TIFF! See you there!" alongside the film's screening schedule.
The Difficult Bride will be screened three times during the festival. The first screening is scheduled for 4pm on September 16, followed by a second screening at 10pm on September 17. The final screening will take place at 12:15pm on September 19.
The first two screenings will be held at TIFF Lightbox Cinema 4 (Paul & Leah Atkinson Family Cinema), while the third will take place at Scotiabank Theatre, Cinema 7.
Set in contemporary Dhaka, The Difficult Bride is a psychological horror film that explores themes of beauty, womanhood, marriage, and societal expectations through a supernatural narrative.
The film stars newcomer Zaineen Chowdhury Karim in the lead role alongside Azmeri Haque Badhan, Reekita Nondine Shimu, Sunerah Binte Kamal, Shatabdi Wadud, Saberi Alam, and Mohammed Bari.
The 51st Toronto International Film Festival will be be held from September 10 to 20.
